title.zh: 中医美容养颜：内调外养，焕发自然美
title.en: TCM Beauty & Skin Care: Inner Balance, Natural Radiance

description.zh: 从中医角度探讨美容养颜的方法，通过内调气血、外养肌肤，实现自然健康的美
description.en: Explore TCM beauty and skin care methods - balance Qi-Blood internally, nourish skin externally for natural healthy beauty

zh.text: 《黄帝内经》中有一句至理名言："夫上古圣人之教下也，皆谓之虚邪贼风，避之有时，恬惔虚无，真气从之，精神内守，病安从来。"这段话揭示了一个核心道理——健康的根本在于内在的调和与养护。中医美容养颜同样遵循这个原则，强调"内调外养"：皮肤的状态不是孤立的，它是身体内部健康状况的晴雨表。通过调理气血、平衡阴阳、养护脏腑，可以从根本上改善皮肤问题，焕发自然健康的美丽。
在临床上，我常常遇到这样的患者：为了脸上的痘痘尝试了各种昂贵的护肤品，甚至去美容院做激光治疗，但效果总是不尽如人意。为什么？因为皮肤问题往往是内在脏腑功能失调的外在投射，只做表面功夫，如同隔靴搔痒。

比如面色萎黄，多半是气血不足，脾失健运，无法将营养物质输送到面部。皮肤干燥起屑，往往与阴虚津亏有关，肺燥不能输布津液到皮毛。反复长痘、痤疮，多见于湿热内蕴的体质，尤其是爱吃辛辣油腻、熬夜的年轻人。皮肤油腻、毛孔粗大，多与痰湿体质有关，脾虚不能运化水湿，湿浊上泛于面。色斑暗沉、黄褐斑，多因肝郁气滞，气血运行不畅，瘀滞于面部络脉所致。至于皱纹早生、皮肤松弛，则往往与肾精不足、气血两虚有关，衰老提前到来。
食疗是中医美容最重要的手段之一。药王孙思邈在《千金要方》中就强调"食治为先"，食疗比药疗更为安全温和，适合长期坚持。针对不同的皮肤问题，饮食调理的方向也各不相同。
对于面色苍白或萎黄、皮肤干燥的人，重点在于养血润肤。红枣是补气养血的代表，每天吃几颗或用红枣泡水，长期坚持能改善面色。桂圆补心脾、益气血，尤其适合操心劳神、失眠多梦的人。黑芝麻补肝肾、益精血，是乌发养颜的佳品。银耳富含天然植物胶质，能滋阴润燥，让皮肤水润饱满。百合养阴润肺、清心安神，适合阴虚燥咳、心烦失眠的人。
对于长痘、皮肤油腻的问题，饮食宜清淡，避免辛辣刺激和甜腻食物。绿豆性凉味甘，能清热解毒、消暑利水，对热性痘痘有很好的缓解作用。苦瓜清热泻火，富含维生素C，能改善痤疮。薏米健脾祛湿，可以减少皮肤出油。冬瓜利水消肿、清热祛湿，适合湿热体质的人。黄瓜清热生津、含水量高，是天然的补水美容食材。
穴位按摩是中医外治法的精华，通过刺激特定穴位，可以调理相应脏腑功能，促进气血运行，改善面部血液循环。下面介绍几个常用的美容穴位，每天花几分钟按揉，长期坚持效果显著。

四白穴（ST2）是美白淡斑的要穴。它位于面部，瞳孔直下，眶下孔凹陷处。每天用食指指腹按揉此穴1-2分钟，能改善眼部周围血液循环，淡化黑眼圈和色斑。迎香穴（LI20）能改善面色，位于鼻翼外缘中点旁、鼻唇沟中。按揉此穴不仅能通鼻窍，还能促进面部气血运行，让面色红润。合谷穴（LI4）被称为"面口合谷收"，意思是头面部的疾病都可以用合谷穴来调理。它位于手背第一、二掌骨之间，按压时会有明显的酸胀感。足三里（ST36）是调理气血的强壮要穴，位于小腿外侧、膝盖下三寸处。常按足三里能健运脾胃、补益气血，从整体上改善肤质。
面部按摩是促进局部气血运行最直接有效的方法。建议每天早晚护肤时，在清洁面部后，用指腹轻轻按压上述穴位，每个穴位按压20-30秒。然后从下巴中央开始，沿着下颌线向上提拉至耳前，再从鼻翼两侧推至太阳穴。按摩的力度要适中，以感觉舒适为度，不可过度用力拉扯皮肤。最后用掌心轻轻拍打全脸，促进血液循环。持之以恒，效果会逐渐显现。

zh.title: 银耳红枣养颜汤
zh.instructions:
1. 银耳泡发撕成小朵
2. 红枣去核
3. 加水炖煮1小时
4. 加入枸杞、冰糖
5. 每日饮用，养血润肤
6. 长期坚持，改善面色

zh.text: 皮肤的健康离不开良好的生活习惯。睡眠是皮肤修复的黄金时间，中医认为夜间是气血回归脏腑的时段，充足的睡眠能让皮肤得到充分的修复和再生。情绪方面，《黄帝内经》说"百病生于气"，情绪的剧烈波动会扰乱气血运行，导致皮肤问题加重。适度运动可以促进全身血液循环，让面色更加红润。此外，我建议尽量减少过度化妆的频率，让皮肤有时间"呼吸"；同时注意防晒和保湿，保护皮肤的屏障功能。这些看似简单的生活细节，恰恰是美容养颜最坚实的基础。
温馨提示：中医美容需要长期坚持，效果需要时间积累。如有严重皮肤问题，建议咨询专业中医师进行辨证论治，配合内服外用综合调理，切勿盲目跟风使用护肤品。

en.text: The Huangdi Neijing contains a timeless teaching: "The sages taught people to avoid deficient and evil winds at the proper times, to maintain tranquility and emptiness, so that genuine Qi follows them, and the spirit is guarded within — where can disease arise?" This reveals a core truth — health is rooted in internal harmony and care. TCM beauty and skincare follow the same principle, emphasizing "inner regulation and outer care." The condition of the skin is never isolated; it is a barometer of the body's internal health. By regulating Qi and Blood, balancing Yin and Yang, and nourishing the internal organs, skin problems can be fundamentally improved, allowing natural, healthy beauty to radiate.

In clinical practice, I frequently encounter patients who have tried every expensive skincare product for their acne, even undergone laser treatments at beauty clinics, yet the results remain unsatisfactory. Why? Because skin problems are often external projections of internal organ dysfunction — treating only the surface is like scratching an itch through one's boot.

A sallow complexion, for instance, usually indicates Qi-Blood deficiency where the spleen fails to transport nutrients to the face. Dry, flaky skin is typically associated with Yin deficiency and fluid depletion — the lung cannot distribute fluids to the skin and body hair. Recurrent acne often reflects a damp-heat constitution, especially common in young people who favor spicy, greasy foods and stay up late. Oily skin with enlarged pores is frequently linked to a phlegm-damp constitution, where the spleen cannot properly metabolize fluids, causing damp turbidity to rise to the face. Dark spots and melasma are most often due to liver Qi stagnation, where Qi and Blood circulation is impeded and accumulates in the facial collaterals. As for early wrinkles and sagging skin, these typically point to kidney essence deficiency and Qi-Blood depletion — aging arriving ahead of schedule.

Food therapy is one of the most important tools in TCM beauty. Sun Simiao, the renowned Tang-dynasty physician, emphasized in his Qian Jin Yao Fang (Essential Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold) that "food therapy comes first" — it is safer and gentler than medication and suitable for long-term adherence. Dietary approaches vary depending on the specific skin concern.

For those with pale or sallow complexions and dry skin, the focus should be on nourishing blood and moisturizing the skin. Red dates are a representative Qi-Blood tonic — eating a few daily or steeping them in hot water can improve complexion over time. Longan tonifies the heart and spleen, benefiting Qi and Blood, especially suitable for those who overthink, worry, and suffer from insomnia. Black sesame tonifies the liver and kidney, benefiting essence and blood — an excellent food for darkening hair and nourishing the face. Tremella is rich in natural plant colloids that nourish Yin and moisten dryness, leaving the skin hydrated and plump. Lily bulb nourishes Yin, moistens the lung, and calms the spirit, ideal for those with Yin-deficiency dry cough and restless sleep.

For acne and oily skin, the diet should be light, avoiding spicy, stimulating, and greasy-sweet foods. Mung beans are cool in nature and sweet in taste, clearing heat, resolving toxins, and relieving summer heat — very effective for heat-type acne. Bitter melon clears heat and drains fire, rich in vitamin C, and helps improve acne. Coix seed strengthens the spleen and resolves dampness, which can reduce skin oiliness. Winter melon drains water, reduces swelling, and clears heat-dampness, suitable for those with damp-heat constitution. Cucumber clears heat, generates fluids, and has high water content — a natural hydrating beauty food.

Acupoint massage is the essence of TCM external therapy. By stimulating specific points, we can regulate the function of corresponding organs, promote Qi-Blood circulation, and improve facial blood flow. Below are several commonly used beauty acupoints. Spend a few minutes each day massaging them, and consistent practice yields remarkable results.

Sibai (ST2) is a key point for whitening and fading spots. Located on the face, directly below the pupil in the infraorbital foramen, daily massage with the index fingertip for 1-2 minutes improves circulation around the eyes and lightens dark circles and pigmentation. Yingxiang (LI20) improves complexion; it lies at the midpoint of the outer edge of the nose wing in the nasolabial groove. Massaging this point not only opens the nasal passages but also promotes facial Qi-Blood circulation, reddening the complexion. Hegu (LI4) is known in TCM as the point that "governs the face and mouth" — disorders of the head and face can be regulated through this point. Located on the dorsum of the hand between the first and second metacarpal bones, pressing here produces a distinct sore, distending sensation. Zusanli (ST36) is a powerful point for regulating Qi and Blood. Located on the outer lower leg, four finger-widths below the knee, regular massage strengthens the spleen and stomach, supplements Qi and Blood, and improves skin quality from the root.

Facial massage is the most direct and effective way to promote local Qi and Blood circulation. I recommend incorporating it into your morning and evening skincare routine. After cleansing, gently press each of the acupoints mentioned above with your fingertips for 20-30 seconds each. Then, starting from the center of the chin, lift upward along the jawline to the front of the ears, then push from the sides of the nose outward to the temples. The pressure should be moderate and comfortable — never pull or drag the skin forcefully. Finish by gently patting the entire face with your palms to stimulate blood circulation. Consistency is key — the results accumulate gradually.

en.title: Tremella Red Date Beauty Soup
en.instructions:
1. Soak tremella, tear into pieces
2. Remove date seeds
3. Simmer for 1 hour
4. Add goji and sugar
5. Drink daily to nourish blood, moisturize skin
6. Long-term practice improves complexion

en.text: Healthy skin depends on good lifestyle habits. Sleep is the prime time for skin repair — TCM holds that nighttime is when Qi and Blood return to the organs, and adequate sleep allows the skin to fully recover and regenerate. Regarding emotions, the Huangdi Neijing states that "all diseases arise from Qi" — intense emotional fluctuations disrupt Qi-Blood circulation, worsening skin problems. Moderate exercise promotes systemic blood circulation, bringing a healthier glow to the complexion. Additionally, I recommend minimizing heavy makeup to let the skin "breathe," and paying attention to sun protection and moisturizing to protect the skin barrier. These seemingly simple lifestyle details are actually the most solid foundation for beauty and skincare.

Note: TCM beauty requires long-term consistency. For severe skin issues, consult a qualified TCM practitioner for pattern differentiation and comprehensive treatment combining internal and external methods. Avoid blindly following skincare trends without professional guidance.
